title: Language, Devices and Their Effects
summary: Every figure of speech and literary device with all the effects you can write, tone and mood word banks, connotation, and a step-by-step method for “explain the effect” questions with model answers.

blocks.text: Writers choose every word on purpose. Language questions in both papers ask you to **spot** a writer’s choice (a simile, a strong verb, a repeated phrase) and, more importantly, to **explain its effect** on the reader. This page gives you every figure of speech and literary device you need, the possible effects of each one, tone and mood word banks, connotation, and a reliable method for “explain the effect” questions with model answers.

blocks.title: How this topic is tested
items: Identify a device: “Give an example of personification from paragraph 3.” / “Tick the device used in line 7.”
Effect of a single word: “Explain the effect of the word ‘…’ in line 12.”
Effect of a phrase or device: “Why does the writer compare the boy to a machine?” / “What is the effect of the simile in line 5?”
Tone and mood: “Which phrase shows the mood changes?” / “What is the writer’s tone in the final paragraph?”
These appear in Paper 2 (fiction) most often, but Paper 1 also asks about the effect of rhetorical questions, emotive words, repetition and headlines.

blocks.text: 1. Naming is not explaining
Naming the device is the doorway. The marks are behind it. Compare:

rows: “The simile ‘the wind howled like a wounded wolf’ makes the storm sound alive, wild and in pain, which makes the night feel dangerous.”
“‘The house watched them leave’ makes the house seem alive and suspicious, so the reader feels the children are not safe even as they escape.”
“Repeating ‘waiting’ three times stretches the moment, so the reader feels how slow and frustrating the delay is.”

blocks.text: 2. Comparisons: simile, metaphor, personification, pathetic fallacy

rows: The lake lay as flat and silver as a mirror.
Says one thing IS another (no like/as)
The classroom was a beehive before the bell.
Gives human actions or feelings to something non-human
The old car coughed and complained up the hill.
Weather or nature reflects a character’s feelings or the mood
As Ali read the letter, grey clouds swallowed the sun.

blocks.title: Why does the author use a simile / metaphor in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To help the reader picture something clearly by comparing it with something familiar.
To make the description more vivid and memorable.
To show a quality of the thing described (size, speed, colour, sound, strength) — say which quality.
To show how a character feels (e.g. “my heart was a drum” shows fear or excitement).
To create a mood (peaceful, threatening, joyful) through the image chosen.
To show the writer’s attitude: a positive comparison praises, a negative one criticises.
A metaphor is stronger than a simile: it says the thing really IS the other thing, so the image feels more powerful and certain.

blocks.title: Why does the author use personification in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To make an object, place or force of nature seem alive.
To make it seem threatening or powerful (a storm that “attacks”), creating fear or tension.
To make it seem friendly or comforting (a house that “welcomes”), creating a warm mood.
To help the reader picture movement or sound vividly.
To reflect the character’s feelings onto the setting.
To make the description more original and engaging than a plain statement.

blocks.title: Why does the author use pathetic fallacy in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To reflect the character’s feelings through the weather (storm = anger or fear, sunshine = happiness).
To create the mood of the scene (gloomy, tense, cheerful).
To foreshadow what will happen next (dark clouds before bad news).
To show a change: when the weather changes, the character’s mood or situation is changing too.

blocks.text: 3. Sound devices

rows: The same sound at the start of nearby words
The silent, silver sea…  /  Big, brave and bold
The same vowel sound repeated inside nearby words
The low, slow moan of the boat
Repeated “s” or “sh” sounds (a type of alliteration/consonance)
The snake slid softly through the sand.
A word that sounds like the noise it describes
crash, sizzle, hiss, thud, buzz, crackle

blocks.title: Why does the author use alliteration / assonance / sibilance in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To draw the reader’s attention to that phrase and make it stand out.
To make the phrase memorable (useful in slogans, headlines and speeches).
To create a rhythm or sound that matches the meaning — hard sounds (b, d, k) feel harsh or forceful, soft sounds (s, l, m) feel calm, gentle or sinister.
Sibilance can suggest whispering, hissing, the sea or a quiet threat.
Long vowel sounds (assonance) can slow the line down and create a sad, calm or heavy mood.
To emphasise the words that carry the key idea.

blocks.title: Why does the author use onomatopoeia in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To let the reader hear the sound, making the scene feel real and immediate.
To make the description more vivid and dramatic.
A sudden loud word (“CRASH!”) can shock the reader or create tension.
A gentle sound (“the kettle hummed”) can create a calm, homely atmosphere.

blocks.text: 4. Exaggeration, imagery and symbolism

rows: I’ve walked a thousand miles today.
Description that appeals to the senses so the reader can imagine it
the sharp smell of lemons and the warm crunch of fresh bread
An object, colour or image that stands for a bigger idea
A locked gate = being shut out · a candle = hope · a white flag = surrender
Lanterns swung in the dark, throwing gold circles on the wall.
Somewhere a dog barked, and the gate creaked.
The kitchen smelled of cumin and burnt sugar.
The tea was sweet and bitter at the same time.
The rope was rough and wet against her palms.

blocks.title: Why does the author use hyperbole / imagery / symbolism in line X? (all possible answers)
items: **Hyperbole:** to emphasise how extreme something is or feels · to show strong emotion (frustration, excitement) · to create humour · in persuasion, to make a problem seem urgent.

**Imagery:** to help the reader imagine the scene with their senses as if they were there · to create atmosphere and mood · to make the description realistic and vivid · to show what a character notices and feels.

**Symbolism:** to suggest a deeper meaning without stating it · to link an object with a feeling or theme (freedom, hope, loss) · to hint at what will happen · to make the reader think more deeply about the message.

blocks.text: 5. Repetition, rhetorical questions and the rule of three

rows: A word, phrase or sentence pattern used again for effect
We waited. We waited all night. We waited until the sky turned grey.
A question asked for effect, not for an answer
How many more trees must we lose before we act?
A list or pattern of three for impact
Our park is cleaner, safer and greener than ever.
Speaking straight to the reader as “you”
You can make a difference today.
Words chosen to make the reader feel strong emotion
helpless, starving puppies abandoned in the cold

blocks.title: Why does the author use repetition in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To emphasise a key idea so the reader cannot miss it.
To show a character’s strong feeling (panic, determination, obsession).
To slow the pace and stretch out a moment (waiting, boredom, dread).
To build tension or rhythm, especially just before a climax.
In persuasion and speeches, to make the message memorable and powerful.

blocks.title: Why does the author use a rhetorical question in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To make the reader stop and think about the issue.
To involve the reader directly, as if in a conversation.
To suggest that the answer is obvious, so the reader agrees with the writer.
To challenge the reader or make them feel responsible (in persuasive writing).
In fiction, to show a character’s confusion, doubt or worry and to create suspense about what will happen.

blocks.title: Why does the author use the rule of three in line X? (all possible answers)
items: To emphasise a point by giving several pieces of support at once.
To create a satisfying, memorable rhythm.
To make the writer sound confident and convincing.
To show how much of something there is (many problems, many benefits).
Often used to build up to the most important idea, placed last.

blocks.text: 6. Contrast, oxymoron and foreshadowing

rows: Placing two very different things close together
Outside, the street was bright and noisy. Inside, the hospital room was dim and silent.
Two opposite words side by side
a deafening silence, bittersweet, a cheerful goodbye
An early hint of what will happen later
Nobody noticed the small crack in the dam that morning.

blocks.title: Why does the author use contrast / oxymoron / foreshadowing in line X? (all possible answers)
items: **Contrast:** to highlight the difference between two people, places or feelings · to make each one stand out more · to show a change (before and after) · to create tension or surprise.
**Oxymoron:** to show mixed or confused feelings · to describe something unusual or hard to put into words · to make the phrase striking and memorable · to make the reader think.

**Foreshadowing:** to create suspense, because the reader expects something to happen · to build a sense of unease or dread · to prepare the reader so the later event feels believable · to make the reader curious about how the hint will connect to the ending.

blocks.text: 7. Tone and mood

rows: How does the writer seem to feel about this?
How does this passage make me feel?
“Fog swallowed the empty platform, and somewhere a train groaned.” (eerie mood)

items: tense / suspenseful
mood: the reader feels something bad may happen soon
eerie / sinister
mood: strange and frightening, as if something is wrong
gloomy / melancholy
mood: sad, dark and heavy
peaceful / serene
mood: calm, quiet and relaxed
joyful / celebratory
mood: happy and full of energy
chaotic
mood: confused, busy and out of control
hopeful
mood or tone: things may get better
nostalgic / wistful
tone: looking back fondly, with some sadness, at the past
sarcastic / mocking
tone: saying the opposite of what is meant to criticise
admiring
tone: full of respect and praise
critical / disapproving
tone: showing faults and dislike
urgent
tone: something must be done now
humorous / playful
tone: light-hearted, aiming to amuse
formal / objective
tone: serious, factual, without personal feeling
bitter
tone: angry and hurt about something unfair

blocks.text: **A mood change** often comes with a change in the setting or the weather, a sudden short sentence, or a new character arriving. When asked which phrase shows the mood changing, look for words such as “Suddenly”, “But then”, “Without warning”, or a change from soft to harsh vocabulary.
8. Connotation: why this word and not another?

**Denotation** is the dictionary meaning of a word. **Connotation** is the feeling or idea the word carries. Writers choose words for their connotations. “The man walked” is neutral. “The man **stormed**” suggests anger. “The man **crept**” suggests secrecy or fear.

blocks.title: Single-word effect method
items: **1. Meaning:** what does the word literally mean here?
**2. Connotation:** what does it suggest or remind us of (danger, softness, power, an animal, a machine)?
**3. Effect:** what does that make the reader picture or feel about this character, place or event?
**4. Compare (optional but strong):** why is it better than a plain word? “‘Crawled’ rather than ‘drove’ suggests the traffic was painfully slow.”

blocks.text: 9. The method for every effect question

items: **Identify** the writer’s choice in the exact lines given (a word, a device, an image, a repetition). If the question names it, start there.
**Quote** it briefly and exactly — one word or a short phrase.
**Say what it does:** what is being compared, exaggerated, repeated or suggested.
**Explain the effect on the reader:** what we picture, feel or understand about the character, setting or idea — be specific to this text.
**Match the marks:** for 2 marks, one point fully explained or two shorter points. For more marks, develop more than one effect (picture + feeling + link to the character or mood).

blocks.title: Vague answers that earn nothing
items: “It makes the reader want to read on.” — true of every text. Instead say what the reader wants to know: “the reader is left wondering who knocked on the door at midnight.”
“It makes it more interesting / exciting / descriptive.” — say how and why.
“It creates a good image.” — say what the image is and what it suggests.
“It emphasises it.” — say what exactly is emphasised and why it matters.
Test: could you write this sentence without reading the text? If yes, it is too vague.

groups.title: Starting your explanation
items: The word “…” suggests that…
The writer compares … to …, which shows…
This makes the reader picture…
This creates a feeling of…
The image of … highlights…

groups.title: Developing the effect
items: This emphasises how … the character feels.
As a result, the setting seems…
This hints that something … is about to happen.
The connotations of “…” are…, so…
This contrasts with…, which makes … stand out.

blocks.text: 10. Model answers
**Text A (fiction):** “The wind clawed at the tent all night. Inside, Tarek lay awake, listening to the canvas snap and shudder like a trapped bird.”
**Question 1:** Explain the effect of the word “clawed”. (1 mark)
**Model:** “Clawed” suggests the wind is a wild animal attacking the tent with sharp claws, which makes the storm seem violent and dangerous.
**Question 2:** Why does the writer compare the canvas to “a trapped bird”? (2 marks)

**Model:** The simile makes the reader picture the canvas flapping wildly and helplessly, like wings beating to escape. It also reflects Tarek’s own feelings: he is stuck inside, frightened and unable to get away from the storm.
**Text B (non-fiction):** “Every year, eight million tonnes of plastic pour into our oceans. Can we really call ourselves the guardians of this planet?”
**Question 3:** Explain the effect of the rhetorical question. (2 marks)

**Model:** The question challenges readers directly and makes them feel guilty, because the answer is clearly “no” after the shocking statistic. The word “guardians” reminds us that we are supposed to protect the planet, so the question pushes readers to take responsibility.

blocks.title: Model longer answer: how is mood created?
blocks.task: Read the paragraph: “The street had emptied by the time Laila turned the corner. A single lamp flickered above the bakery, its light trembling on the wet stones. Somewhere behind her, footsteps stopped when she stopped. She walked faster. So did they.” How does the writer create a tense mood in this paragraph? Refer to the writer’s use of language. (4 marks)
text: The writer creates tension first through the setting. The street had “emptied”, so Laila is alone, and the reader feels she is vulnerable because nobody could help her.

The image of a lamp that “flickered” with light “trembling on the wet stones” is personification: the light seems nervous, as if it is shaking with fear, and because it could go out at any moment, the reader worries Laila will be left in darkness.

Finally, the short sentences “She walked faster. So did they.” speed up the pace and copy her quick steps. The repetition of the pattern shows that the unseen follower is copying her exactly, which makes the reader fear she is being chased.
blocks.marks: 4/4 (three language choices quoted, each effect explained precisely)
notes: Each point quotes a short, exact piece of evidence (“emptied”, “flickered”, “trembling”, “She walked faster. So did they.”).
Devices are named (personification, short sentences, repetition) but the focus is on the effect.
Effects are specific to this text (alone, darkness, being chased), never “it makes it exciting”.
Every point links back to the question’s focus: a tense mood.
Written in clear paragraphs, one language choice per paragraph.

blocks.text: 11. Practice questions

items.q: Name the device: “The traffic crawled along the bridge like a tired snail.” Give two possible effects.
items.a: Simile. Effects: it helps the reader picture how slowly the traffic moved, and it creates a feeling of frustration and boredom (“tired” suggests the drivers are worn out).

items.q: Name the device: “Her words were knives.” Why might the writer use it?
items.a: Metaphor. It shows her words hurt deeply and sharply, as if they cut the listener. Saying the words ARE knives makes the hurt seem stronger than a simile would.

items.q: “The sea swallowed the little boat.” Explain the effect of “swallowed”.
items.a: “Swallowed” makes the sea seem like a huge, hungry creature that eats the boat completely, suggesting the boat disappeared suddenly and the sea is powerful and dangerous.

items.q: “The sun smiled on the children as they ran out of school.” Name the device and give two possible effects.
items.a: Personification. It makes the weather seem friendly and warm, and it creates a happy, carefree mood that matches the children’s feelings at the end of the school day.

items.q: “Rain hammered on the roof as Nour read the hospital report.” What is the device and why is it used?
items.a: Pathetic fallacy. The violent rain reflects Nour’s worry and shock and creates a gloomy, tense mood. It may also hint that the news is bad.

items.q: “Crack! The branch gave way.” Why does the writer use onomatopoeia here?
items.a: So the reader hears the sudden sound, which makes the moment feel immediate and shocking and builds tension about whether someone will fall.

items.q: “Soft, silent snowflakes settled on the sleeping city.” Name the sound device and its effect.
items.a: Sibilance / alliteration with the “s” sound. The soft hissing sound matches the quiet snowfall and creates a calm, peaceful mood.

items.q: “I’m so hungry I could eat a camel!” Name the device and say why it is used.
items.a: Hyperbole. It exaggerates to show how extremely hungry the speaker feels and adds humour.

items.q: “We need cleaner air, safer streets and greener parks.” Name the device and give two effects.
items.a: Rule of three. It emphasises how many improvements are needed and creates a memorable rhythm that makes the writer sound confident and persuasive.

items.q: “Do we want our grandchildren to ask why we did nothing?” Why does the writer use this question?
items.a: It is a rhetorical question that makes readers imagine being blamed in the future, so they feel guilty and responsible, and the obvious answer (“no”) pushes them to agree they must act.

items.q: “It was a sweet sorrow to leave the village.” Name the device and explain.
items.a: Oxymoron (“sweet sorrow”). It shows mixed feelings: sad to leave, but with happy memories or excitement about the future.

items.q: “Nobody locked the back door that night.” What might this sentence do near the start of a story?
items.a: It foreshadows trouble, such as a break-in. It creates suspense because the reader expects the unlocked door to matter later.

items.q: Explain the connotations: “The children swarmed into the playground.”
items.a: “Swarmed” suggests insects such as bees, so the children seem noisy, numerous and uncontrollable, moving all at once.

items.q: Identify the tone: “Oh brilliant, the lift is broken again. Ten floors of stairs — just what I needed.”
items.a: Sarcastic: the speaker says “brilliant” and “just what I needed” but means the opposite, showing annoyance.

items.q: What mood is created? “Lanterns glowed along the river, and the smell of roasted corn drifted between the laughing families.”
items.a: A warm, joyful and peaceful mood, created by soft light (“glowed”), pleasant smells and the sound of “laughing families”.

items.q: A student answers: “The simile makes the reader want to read on.” Rewrite it for the simile “the corridor stretched ahead like a dark throat”.
items.a: Example: The simile makes the corridor seem like the inside of a creature’s mouth, as if it could swallow the character. This creates fear, and the reader worries about what waits at the end of the corridor.

items.q: “The head teacher’s voice cut through the noise.” Explain the effect of “cut”.
items.a: “Cut” suggests something sharp and sudden, so her voice is clear, firm and powerful enough to stop the noise immediately, which shows her authority.

items.q: Symbolism: In a story, a girl keeps her late grandmother’s key on a chain around her neck. What might the key symbolise?
items.a: It may symbolise her connection to her grandmother, her memories, or a family home and belonging that she does not want to lose.
